newsitem.title: USA: Teamster president calls for striker rallies.
newsitem.headline: Teamster president calls for striker rallies.

text.p: United Parcel Service and the Teamsters stepped up negotiations Friday, but union president Ron Carey said strikers must win the bitter dispute on the picket lines.

With the strike in its 12th day, the nation's biggest package delivery service and its second-largest union redoubled their efforts to reach a settlement, said Susan King, spokeswoman for Labor Secretary Alexis Herman.

Carey paid compliments to Herman and a federal mediator for their efforts to settle the strike, but called a news conference and said there would be two dozen rallies in the United States next week, with similar events in Europe, to drum up support for the 185,000 workers on strike.

"A contract that provides the good jobs for working families certainly won't be won at the bargaining table," he told reporters. "The only way you can win that is either on the picket lines, and in the community."
The two sides talked all Friday after meeting from morning until well after midnight Thursday. They broke to sleep and analyze numbers that came up in the talks.

"We think the fact that they've been sitting for 20-1/2 hours talking, crunching numbers, moving back and forth between ... rooms (means it) is clear that they are redoubling their efforts," King said.
At the White House, spokesman Mike McCurry declined to characterize the talks but noted: "They're talking and that's good." United Parcel Service made no comment as the talks continued.
Cornell University labor studies professor Richard Hurd said the union's tough stance was necessary for morale, and did not read it as a sign talks were faltering.

"Unions have to be very careful in how they publicly respond to management overtures in a strike situation, because if they get the hopes of the strikers up and then nothing happens, morale plummets," he said.
The strike was causing severe problems for some businesses and a blood bank.

A major U.S. blood bank reported it has destroyed more than 800 pints of blood because overburdened delivery companies Federal Express Corp. and Airborne Express could no longer guarantee their usual overnight delivery.
The group, America's Blood Centers, suggested its blood banks set up mobile collection units near UPS picket lines so that striking UPS workers can donate blood.

The UPS workers have been on strike since Aug. 4 to demand full-time status and benefits for some of the company's many part-time employees. The walkout is the biggest since a three-day strike by 400,000 Teamster truckers in 1976, Hurd said.
The strike is putting increasing pressure on both sides.

The company estimates it is losing $300 million a week, putting its losses so far at about $500 million or more. UPS carried 80 percent of the small packages in the United States before the strike. It has tried to keep priority deliveries such as medical supplies going with management help, but its volume has shrunk to about 10 percent of normal.
The strikers are getting help from other unions, but finding it tough to live on $55-a-week strike benefits.

Opinion polls suggest the public sympathizes more with the strikers than with the company. Many small businesses are feeling the pinch of being unable to deliver their goods. Some have laid off workers or lost substantial business.

UPS competitors have rushed to try to fill the void. The U.S. Postal Service said Friday it would continue Sunday deliveries in some areas of the United States to handle increased mail volume as a result of the strike.

Until late this week, UPS took a hard line in the negotiations, insisting that the union put the company's last contract offer to a membership vote and calling on President Bill Clinton to use his powers to stop the strike.
But Clinton has refused to intervene and UPS appeared to soften its stance Thursday, suggesting its "final" offer was negotiable.
